outlier.evidence: Ratings 4, 5, 6, 7 spread evenly, two on each side of the threshold. The lowest, Reviewer_xTkz (4), is weak, but Reviewer_P8h7 (5, confidence 4) argues for rejection independently and on checkable grounds.

inattentive_reviews.evidence: Its limitations section repeats its main review almost word for word. It asks why a model is needed when a script can produce the trajectories, an objection that applies to every synthetic benchmark (CLEVR, gSCAN, BabyAI). It credits the generalization to 'the Transformer', but the paper's SFT transformers score at or below the LSTM baselines (lines 221-223). It asks how descriptions are generated, which lines 103-105 answer at a high level. It never replied to the rebuttal and edited its review on 2021-08-31 with no comment.

checkable_claims.claim: The paper's statement that prior meanings 'rarely consider spatial reference to objects' is false; Touchdown and similar instruction-following datasets require complex spatial relations.
checkable_claims.evidence: Lines 307-308: 'Meanings typically refer to instantaneous actions and rarely consider spatial reference to objects [32]'. The submission cites neither Touchdown, Room2Room nor ALFRED; its navigation citations are [8, 9]. The camera-ready keeps the sentence and still cites none of the three.

checkable_claims.claim: The 'Natural English version' row of Figure 1 is never used.
checkable_claims.evidence: All data come from the templated grammar (vocabulary 53, maximum length 8; lines 106-109). The text never uses the English row, and the submitted caption does not call it illustrative. The authors confirmed it is illustrative only, and the camera-ready caption says so.

checkable_claims.claim: There are no baselines that see only one modality and no error analysis.
checkable_claims.evidence: Section 3 reports only per-category F1 for six Transformer variants and two LSTM baselines (Figs. 3-4). No single-modality model or error breakdown exists, and the rebuttal did not add one.

checkable_claims.claim: The systematic-generalization tests withhold only one to three word combinations per split.
checkable_claims.evidence: Lines 255-270: split 1 removes 'red cat', 'blue door' and 'green cactus'; split 2 removes 'grow' with the plant category; splits 3-5 each remove one construction ('right of', 'was left of', 'was grasp'). One train set serves all five splits (line 271).

checkable_claims.claim: Details of how the trajectories and descriptions are generated are missing.
checkable_claims.evidence: For trajectories the main text says only 'We use a bot to generate the episodes' (line 194) and defers to Supplementary Section 2.1. The grammar is described (lines 103-141), with its BNF in the supplement. The authors conceded 'insufficient details on trajectory generation'.

checkable_claims.claim: The good generalization comes from the Transformer, whose generalization is already known, so the method is not novel.
checkable_claims.evidence: The paper's result is that Transformer structure matters. SFT variants 'perform poorly on all test categories, in line or worse than the baselines' (lines 221-223): 0.75 against 0.80 for LSTMs on spatio-temporal sentences, and about 0.36 and 0.11 on systematic splits 3 and 5 (Fig. 4).

checkable_claims.claim: Models reach near-ceiling performance in a number of conditions, so the dataset may be too easy.
checkable_claims.evidence: UT and TFT reach 1.0 +/- 0.003 on Basic sentences (line 236) and about 0.96-0.98 on systematic splits 1-2 (Fig. 4; lines 276-277, 'solved'). Its stronger phrase, near-ceiling 'in the most challenging conditions', overstates: the best model reaches about 0.77, 0.79 and 0.86 on splits 3-5. Zjb3 itself called the concern 'not too crucial'.

checkable_claims.claim: The TFT models are almost at 100% F1, which suggests the task is too easy to test all aspects of spatio-temporal grounding.
checkable_claims.evidence: True only for the easy sets: TFT is about 1.0 on Basic and 0.95-0.97 on Spatial and Temporal (Fig. 3) and 0.97-0.98 on systematic splits 1-2 (Fig. 4). It is about 0.90 on Spatio-temporal sentences, and about 0.77, 0.79 and 0.22 on systematic splits 3-5 (TFT-WA about 0.57, 0.58, 0.73). Lines 278-279: 'the scores overall drop significantly'.

rebuttal.evidence: Reviewer_3aA5 (2021-09-01): 'I will not increase my score'; its review is unedited at 6. Reviewer_P8h7 (2021-08-15): 'I am still leaning towards rejection'; it edited its review the same day and ends at 5, below the threshold. Reviewer_xTkz edited on 2021-08-31 with no comment and ends at 4. Reviewer_Zjb3 never posted and is unedited at 7. No reviewer states a score change, and no edit crossed the threshold.
rebuttal.what_convinced_or_not: The motivation reply 'clarifies the motivation a bit' for P8h7, which then asked for the truth function to be tested as an RL reward and with natural language; the authors declined RL experiments as orthogonal. The hard-negative controls 'ease some of' 3aA5's generalization concerns. 3aA5 still kept 6: without vocabulary scaling or real-language tests it found the task's utility unclear, and it cited the other reviewers. It had first called the motivation 'quite clear'. xTkz never answered the reply on positioning and on the scripted oracle.

ac.evidence: Ratings split two and two (mean 5.5). The AC followed the post-rebuttal comments of P8h7 and 3aA5 (synthetic task, unclear link to realistic settings) and xTkz's comparison with ALFRED, and set aside Zjb3's 7 and 3aA5's numeric 6. It added its own reading: the paper 'feels too preliminary', and TFT is 'almost at 100% F1', which Fig. 4 contradicts for splits 3-5. It credits 'one of the reviewers' with suggesting re-use of ALFRED data; 3aA5 suggested a zero-shot test on Room2Room, marked '(Minor)'.

main_reasons_for_decision: Synthetic benchmark with no shown link to realistic settings or natural language (P8h7, 3aA5, AC)
Weak positioning against existing benchmarks such as ALFRED, Room2Room and CLEVRER (P8h7, xTkz, AC)
AC's own reading: 'too preliminary', and near-100% TFT F1 suggests the task is too easy
No reviewer argued for the paper after the rebuttal; 3aA5 declined to raise and P8h7 stayed below threshold

outlier.evidence: 4 against 6, 6, 7. Its core objection (structured synthetic language, toy environment, a 'somewhat obvious' object-identity result) is a judgement Committee A shared. Two side points are wrong: one-hot words pass through a learned projection (lines 149, 171-172), and compositional grounding work is cited. It spent 2 hours and wrote 'YES' for limitations. It never posted publicly; the AC reports that it later called its objection 'a corner case' and 'marginally below threshold'.

inattentive_reviews.evidence: A 7 whose main review restates the abstract and adds 'clearly written, well-organized'. It lists no weakness and no question, says limitations 'are described in the Conclusions', and never posted in the discussion, although it reports 6 hours. Its 7 carries no argument.

checkable_claims.claim: Words and sentences are represented as one-hot vectors rather than embeddings, which fixes the dictionary.
checkable_claims.evidence: Line 149 defines each word as a one-hot vector, and lines 171-172 project the inputs 'to a common dimension' before the Transformer, which is a learned embedding. The authors explained this. Only the fixed-dictionary point stands, and it would need pretrained embeddings.

checkable_claims.claim: Related work on compositional grounded language learning is missing.
checkable_claims.evidence: The submission cites gSCAN [34], Hill et al. [22], Hupkes et al. [25], Lake and Baroni [26], Sugita and Tani [37] and Tuci et al. [40] on compositional or systematic grounded language. Its other point holds: Tenbrink is not cited; the camera-ready adds [43, 44].

checkable_claims.claim: Negatives are random, which may be too easy.
checkable_claims.evidence: Lines 197-199: each observation is paired with a true sentence or 'another false sentence generated from the grammar'. The authors ran hard-negative tests in the rebuttal and added one to the camera-ready (Fig. 5).

checkable_claims.claim: The paper does not explain how animals move.
checkable_claims.evidence: Line 101 says only that 'the animals can move independently'. The authors added the mechanism to the supplement.

checkable_claims.claim: How negative sentences are generated is not described, and Supplementary Section 2.1 does not explain it.
checkable_claims.evidence: The main text gives one clause, 'another false sentence generated from the grammar' (lines 198-199). The supplement is not part of the submitted PDF, so that part was not checked; the authors replied that they added the explanation to it.

checkable_claims.claim: The synthetic language is unambiguous, neatly structured and semantically homogeneous.
checkable_claims.evidence: Templated grammar with a 53-word vocabulary and sentences of at most 8 words (lines 106-109), in four fixed sentence types (lines 113-141).

rebuttal.evidence: Reviewer_viF6 (2021-08-29): 'I am raising the score to marginally above acceptance'; edited the same day, now 6. Reviewer_MYUM's posted 4 is unedited, but the AC reports that MYUM said in discussion that it 'voted marginally below threshold' and reads the 4 as '5+'; that move is effective only. Reviewer_8BQz (2021-08-27): 'happy to raise the score' if its questions were clarified; the authors answered on 2021-08-31, but the review was never edited and stays 6. Reviewer_3pgx never posted.
rebuttal.what_convinced_or_not: viF6 was moved by the answers on data generation, negatives, animal motion and contributions ('Authors have addressed all of the concerns'), though it kept MYUM's concern about the simple environment. 8BQz accepted the truth-function motivation and welcomed the hard-negative tests it had asked for: under 5% drop with hard trajectories, about 0.3 drop on splits 1-2 with shuffled words. MYUM, per the AC, kept its objection but called it 'a corner case'.

ac.evidence: Three reviewers at 6, 6, 7 after discussion. The AC reads MYUM's unedited 4 as '5+' from MYUM's discussion comment, names the toy synthetic language as 'the main objection', and judges such testbeds important 'if they serve as a starting point'. It closes on 'the reviewer consensus post discussion' and 'I don't think anyone is looking to champion the case for rejecting it'.

main_reasons_for_decision: Three of four reviewers above threshold after discussion; viF6 raised to 6
AC judged the toy synthetic language acceptable for a testbed that opens a new direction
AC read MYUM's 4 as 5+, so no reviewer championed rejection
The rebuttal supplied the hard-negative tests that 8BQz asked for

issues_only_a: Positioning against ALFRED, Room2Room, Touchdown and CLEVRER, and the overstated claim that prior work rarely uses spatial reference (P8h7, xTkz, AC)
No demonstration of the truth function as an RL reward (P8h7)
No ablation over vocabulary size or number of withheld combinations, and no zero-shot real-language test (3aA5, AC)
Near-ceiling scores suggest the task is too easy (Zjb3, AC)
No single-modality baselines or error analysis (P8h7)
Why learn a truth function when a script can produce the trajectories (xTkz)
Arbitrary line between temporal and instantaneous predicates (3aA5)
issues_only_b: The main finding, that object identity matters, is obvious (MYUM)
A binary truth function is a narrow form of semantics; why not generate descriptions (8BQz, MYUM)
One-hot word representation instead of embeddings (MYUM; a misreading)
Missing literature on spatial and temporal prepositions, e.g. Tenbrink (MYUM)
shared_issues: Synthetic, templated language and a toy 2D world, with unclear transfer to natural language (P8h7, Zjb3, 3aA5, xTkz in A; 8BQz, viF6, MYUM in B; both ACs)
Shortcut learning against compositional understanding: proxy features or random negatives (3aA5 in A; 8BQz in B), answered in both with the same hard-negative tests
Missing data-generation details: bot trajectories, negatives, animal motion (xTkz in A; viF6 in B)
Unclear writing and operator notation (P8h7, xTkz in A; viF6 in B)
Whether the 'Natural English version' in Figure 1 is used (P8h7 in A; 8BQz in B)
Novelty relative to prior grounding work (P8h7, xTkz in A; viF6, MYUM in B)
verdict: Both committees saw the same facts and weighted them differently. Ratings were almost the same: A gave 5, 7, 6, 4 (mean 5.5) and B gave 6, 6, 7, 4 (mean 5.75). Every reviewer who listed a weakness named the synthetic, templated language or the toy 2D world, and nobody found a technical error. In A, the rebuttal moved nobody toward acceptance: Reviewer_P8h7 stayed 'leaning towards rejection' and asked for an RL test, Reviewer_3aA5 kept 6 but adopted the other reviewers' utility concern, and neither Reviewer_xTkz (4) nor Reviewer_Zjb3 (7) posted again. A's AC then added its own reason, that TFT is 'almost at 100% F1' so the task may be too easy; Fig. 4 of the submission contradicts this, with TFT at about 0.77, 0.79 and 0.22 on systematic splits 3 to 5. A's detractors also attacked the paper's positioning against ALFRED, Room2Room and Touchdown, which it does not cite; that point is correct, and no rebuttal experiment could answer it. In B, the rebuttal landed: Reviewer_viF6 raised to 6, Reviewer_8BQz got the hard-negative tests it asked for, and the AC read Reviewer_MYUM's unedited 4 as '5+' from discussion and called the toy language acceptable for a testbed. B's support is thinner than its scores: confidences 3, 2, 3, 3, and Reviewer_3pgx's 7 lists no weakness. The split is a different tolerance for a synthetic benchmark. A's post-rebuttal comments and AC held it against the paper; B's did not.
